This lab has exercises that reinforce the section "Working on remote machines" of Lecture 4 (`lectures/lec04_remote_machines_postgres.qmd`) and the sections "Finding and stopping a process" and "Background job administration" of Lecture 2 (`lectures/lec02_linux_advanced.qmd`). Parts 1 and 2 get you onto Moriah, the HUJI cluster, and move files back and forth. In Parts 3 to 7 you run **everything on Moriah**. You will need a second terminal logged into Moriah in a few places.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Ground rules
* Run every command yourself. Many answers depend on what you see (and your PID numbers will not be the same as anyone else's).
* Leave the "#TODO text [question text] text" line and start a new line underneath and write your answers on that new line
* This file stays on your laptop, and you commit and push it from there. Keep it open on your laptop while your terminal is on Moriah.
* Moriah is **shared** and its login machine is used by everyone. Other people's programs will show up in your output, including your classmates' `sleep` commands from this very lab. Only ever touch your own processes. Run nothing heavy on the login machine: everything here just sleeps or prints a line per second.
* Clean up after yourself. Every part ends by stopping the processes it started. Check with `pgrep -u $USER -a sleep` that none are left over.
* **Never** put your private key (`~/.ssh/id_ed25519`) in this file or anywhere else.
:::

`sleep 600` does nothing for 10 minutes, which makes it a perfect process to look at. The `&` at the end runs it in the **background**, so you get your prompt back. The shell stores the PID of the last background process in the variable `$!`:

```bash

echo $!
```

# Part 5: Signals and `kill`

`kill` sends a **signal** to a process. A process killed by signal number *n* has exit status 128 + *n*. List all of the signals and find the numbers of `HUP`, `INT`, `KILL`, `TERM`, `STOP` and `CONT`:

```bash
kill -l
```

Create a program that refuses to die when it is politely asked to stop. The `trap '' TERM` line tells bash to ignore the TERM signal:

```bash
cat > stubborn.sh << 'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
trap '' TERM
while true; do sleep 1; done
EOF
chmod +x stubborn.sh
./stubborn.sh &
echo $!
```

Ask it to stop (the default signal of `kill` is TERM) and look at it:

```bash
kill $!
sleep 2
ps -o pid,stat,command -p $!
```

#TODO [is the process still there, and why? <1pts>]
#TODO [write the command that stops it for sure, and the command that proves that it is gone <1pts>]

Use `wait` to get the exit status of processes that were killed by different signals. `wait PID` waits for that process and then sets `$?` to its exit status:

```bash
sleep 600 &
kill $!
wait $!
echo $?

sleep 600 &
kill -9 $!
wait $!
echo $?
```

#TODO [the two exit statuses that you got, and which signal numbers do they correspond to? <2pts>]

A process can be paused without dying. `STOP` suspends it and `CONT` resumes it. This is the signal that Ctrl+Z sends (almost; Ctrl+Z sends a variant called `TSTP`):

```bash
sleep 600 &
kill -STOP $!
ps -o pid,stat,command -p $!
kill -CONT $!
ps -o pid,stat,command -p $!
kill $!
```

#TODO [what was the `STAT` in each of the two `ps` lines? <1pts>]
#TODO [`stubborn.sh` ignored TERM. Try to make it ignore `KILL` by editing the `trap` line: what happens, and why does that explain what `kill -9` is for? <2pts>]

There is also `pkill`, which kills by *name* instead of by PID. Moriah is exactly the kind of machine where you must think before you use it. **Do not run this one**, just think about it:

```bash
pkill -x sleep       # -x : the process name must match exactly
```

# Part 6: Surviving a logout with `nohup`

When you close a terminal, the system sends the **HUP** ("hang-up") signal to the programs that were started from it, and by default they die. `nohup` makes a program ignore HUP. You can test that without closing anything, by sending HUP yourself:

```bash
sleep 600 &
echo $!
nohup sleep 601 > /dev/null 2>&1 &
echo $!
```

#TODO [what does `> /dev/null 2>&1` do, and why does `nohup` need it in this line? <1pts>]

Send the HUP signal to both processes and see which ones survive. Use `wait` on the first one to see its exit status:

```bash
#TODO [command that sends HUP to the two sleeps you just started <1pts>]
pgrep -u $USER -a sleep
```

#TODO [which process died and which survived? What was the exit status of the one that died (use `wait`) and why? <2pts>]

Clean up what is left:

```bash
pkill -u $USER -x sleep
```

Now a realistic job. This script is a stand-in for a long computation: it writes the date to the standard output every second.

```bash
cat > infinite_loop.sh << 'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
while true; do date; sleep 1; done
EOF
chmod +x infinite_loop.sh
```

Start it so that it survives logging out, and so that its output is saved:

```bash
#TODO [command that runs infinite_loop.sh with nohup in the background, saving all its output (including errors) to out.log <2pts>]
```

# Part 7: A terminal that survives: `tmux`

`nohup` keeps one command alive. `tmux` keeps a whole **terminal** alive, so that you can go away and come back to see it as you left it. Start a session called `lab4` on Moriah (if you get `command not found`, look for it with `module spider tmux`, as in the lecture):

```bash
tmux new -s lab4
```

You are now inside tmux (note the green bar at the bottom). Inside it, start the loop in the background and look at it:

```bash
cd ~/lab04
./infinite_loop.sh > out.log 2>&1 &
tail -n 2 out.log
```

Detach: press Ctrl+B, release both keys, then press d. You are back in your normal terminal on Moriah. Look at the session and at the job, and then come back:

```bash
tmux ls
pgrep -u $USER -af infinite_loop
jobs
tmux attach -t lab4
jobs
```

#TODO [paste the line that `tmux ls` printed. Why did `jobs` print nothing in the normal terminal but print the job after you attached? <1pts>]

Detach again. Now really leave: run `exit` to log out of Moriah, so that you are back on your laptop. Run `tmux ls` on your laptop, then log in again and reattach:

```bash
tmux ls                     # on your laptop
ssh moriah
tmux ls                     # on Moriah
tmux attach -t lab4
tail -n 2 out.log
```

#TODO [what did `tmux ls` print on the laptop versus on Moriah, and why? Where does the session live? <1pts>]

Inside the session, press Ctrl+B and then c to create a second tabbed window, and Ctrl+B and then n / p to move between the two. Then detach again and kill the whole session from outside:

```bash
tmux kill-session -t lab4
tmux ls
pgrep -u $USER -af infinite_loop
```
